summary.title: Teach Yourself Programming in Ten Years
summary.one_liner: Programming expertise takes years of deliberate practice rather than a 24-hour or 21-day crash course, and Norvig lays out a practical path for getting there.
keywords: structure and interpretation of computer programs
takeaways: Learning to program well takes sustained practice over years; quick books only teach superficial syntax.
Deliberate practice means working on tasks just beyond your ability, getting feedback, and correcting errors.
Learn by doing, talk with other programmers, read others' code, and work on projects alongside and after others.
Learn at least six languages spanning class, functional, syntactic, declarative and parallel abstraction styles.
Pick a first language that is simple, interactive, and popular in a community you can learn from.
summary.summary: Peter Norvig argues that the market for 'Teach Yourself X in 24 Hours' books reflects unrealistic expectations, and he draws on research on expert performance (Bloom, Ericsson, Gladwell's 10,000-hour idea) to argue that mastery takes about ten years of deliberate practice. He gives a personal recipe for programming success covering projects, reading code, learning several languages, and contributing to standards efforts. The essay closes with advice on choosing a first language (use what your friends use, keep it simple, prefer interactive mode) and a short annotated list of books such as SICP, How to Design Programs, and Oz.
